item.title: Sam Altman clarifies remarks on memory and local AI
item.description:
Sam Altman clarifies remarks on memory and local AI

Sam Altman has addressed the context of his previous comments regarding personal computer memory and data centers, clarifying that his remarks about centralizing memory usage were misinterpreted.

📢 New Clarifications

Speaking onstage at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World summit on Monday, Altman stated that he wants people to have a lot of RAM and that everybody should be able to buy a lot of RAM for their own computer. He also noted that “home tinkering is great.”

These comments follow his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he said it’s “quite terrible” for everyone to have RAM in personal computers rather than in data centers. Altman previously stated on X that the original remarks had been “taken out of context” and reiterated his desire for users to have “so much ram.”

🔍 The Context

  • Memory Usage: Altman suggested that “share this memory” and explained that if the world is in a memory supply shortage, it might be optimal to have memory working 100 percent of the time rather than sometimes off in someone’s edge device.
  • Misinterpretation: Altman stated, “That comment, which I think got misinterpreted, but there is a true part of it, which I will stand by,” explaining that he was trying to discuss the optimal use of limited supply, though he noted that people having their own at-home inference is a tradeoff.
  • Supply Chain Issues: Altman commented that OpenAI has “been constrained by different things at different times,” including memory, rack assembly, data center capacity, or “some random component.”
  • Supply Shortage: He noted that “a few years ago we started saying the world needs to build a lot more memory supply chain in particular,” but “the world did not build out that much,” resulting in DRAM prices potentially going up “5x, 7x, something like that.”
  • Jensen Huang: Altman also commented on Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia’s CEO, saying he “doesn’t know enough” to say if Huang should be reinstated.

💡 Why It Matters

AI companies have been buying up the world’s memory supply for data centers, leading to ongoing price hikes on everything from phones to game consoles. Altman’s clarifications highlight the tension between the need for centralized data center memory and the value of personal computer hardware for local inference.

#OpenAI #AI #SAM-Altman #Memory-Shortage #Data-Centers #Tech

Source: Sam Altman says he wants everyone ‘to have a lot of RAM’

item.title: OpenAI’s RAM Buying Spree Tightens Global Memory Supply
item.description:
OpenAI’s RAM Buying Spree Tightens Global Memory Supply

OpenAI’s rapid acquisition of DRAM has drawn attention to a growing shortage of RAM worldwide. CEO Sam Altman warned that keeping large amounts of memory in personal computers is “terrible” when the same chips could be better utilized in data‑center clouds.

🔍 Overview

OpenAI is buying massive quantities of DRAM for its cloud‑based AI workloads. The company’s purchasing power has led to long‑term contracts with the biggest memory manufacturers, effectively reserving a large share of the world’s RAM output for the next few years.

📦 Supply Chain Impact

  • OpenAI’s buying spree is squeezing the world’s supply of RAM.
  • Samsung and SK Hynix have signed long‑term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate, reserving much of the upcoming RAM production.
  • The billions of dollars spent on chips are a factor behind rising prices for laptops, phones, and other consumer devices.

🖥️ Why Data‑Center RAM Matters

“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open‑source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center. But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time. You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply‑constrained environment.”

Altman argues that keeping DRAM idle in personal machines wastes scarce resources; cloud‑scale deployment yields far higher utilization.

💰 Economic Ripple

  • The high demand for RAM by AI developers translates into higher hardware costs for everyday consumers.
  • As memory manufacturers allocate more production to cloud operators, smaller‑scale buyers face tighter inventories and price pressure.

The situation highlights a broader tension between the push for local AI inference and the physical limits of global memory supply.

#OpenAI #RAM #SupplyChain #DataCenters

Source: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk

item.title: NVIDIA Partners with Palantir to Optimize Global Supply Chain Decisions
item.description:
NVIDIA Partners with Palantir to Optimize Global Supply Chain Decisions

NVIDIA’s supply chain operations team has collaborated with Palantir to build a unified Digital Supply Chain Intelligence command center. By linking Palantir Foundry’s Ontology with NVIDIA cuOpt decision optimization, the system provides a comprehensive view of global manufacturing inputs. This integration helps planners resolve complex material allocations and streamline production timelines.

🔍 Overview

NVIDIA operates one of the world’s largest and most complex supply chains, measuring performance from the moment silicon leaves the fab to the deployment of productive data centers. Supply chain efficiency is tracked using several distinct metrics:

Metric Scope and Definition
Time-to-rack From the moment silicon leaves the fab to the arrival of an assembled system on a data center floor.
Time-to-token Covers everything after time-to-rack, including power, cooling, networking, and the software stack that enables day-one productivity.
Time of Ownership (TOO) The time elapsed from the moment a manufacturing site receives material to when it leaves as part of a sub-assembly or finished product.

⚙️ Key details

Managing materials across a global footprint involves highly volatile components and constraints:

  • Platform scale: The NVIDIA Grace Blackwell NVL72 platform incorporates millions of parts and thousands of global suppliers, with final systems built by dozens of OEMs and ODMs. A single rack holds eighteen compute trays; just one of these trays requires two NVIDIA Grace CPUs, four NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, and thirty-two HBM3e stacks.
  • Expanding footprint: The supply chain developed for the Vera Rubin platform is twice as large as that of the Grace Blackwell.
  • Weekly volatility: Critical components—including CPUs, GPUs, and memory—face fluctuating weekly availability. A part that delays a build one week may be freely available the next, with each component carrying its own bill of materials, suppliers, and lead times.
  • Assembly requirements: Contract manufacturers are restricted from starting assembly until all components have arrived from three distinct pools: parts shipped directly from NVIDIA, consignment parts stocked by NVIDIA, and parts sourced from suppliers.
  • Allocation windows: Material allocation spans the current and subsequent quarter. The nearest weeks are already committed, meaning new weekly data primarily impacts decisions further out.

🧩 How it works

The Digital Supply Chain Intelligence command center surfaces previously buried risks, blockers, and signals by combining two main software technologies:

Palantir Foundry

Palantir Foundry provides the underlying operating context. Its “Ontology” serves as a governed data layer connecting materials, manufacturing sites, commits, capacity, allocations, production outputs, and qualitative signals. Composed of objects and links rather than standard rows and tables, this Ontology forms a complete representation of operational reality.

NVIDIA cuOpt

NVIDIA cuOpt, an open-source library for GPU-accelerated decision optimization, draws inputs directly from the Ontology. It models material allocation as a mixed-integer linear program to minimize Time of Ownership (TOO), determining how much constrained material should go to which manufacturing sites and when. Once solved, cuOpt writes the allocation decision back to the Ontology.

💡 Why it matters

Integrating optimization software directly into the supply chain context provides several operational advantages:

  • Scenario simulation: Planners can simulate and analyze various scenarios within the Ontology, giving them wider access to the decision space and laying the foundation for an AI flywheel that improves performance over time.
  • Constraint identification: Beyond generating allocation schedules, cuOpt reports exactly which constraints are binding. This allows planners to see, for example, if Taiwan capacity rather than memory supply held down a specific week’s output.
  • Exploratory planning: Because the optimization solving speed is fast, planners can easily explore the surrounding decision space.
  • Capturing the human factor: By back-testing historical decisions against actual outcomes, NVIDIA and Palantir identified a human factor that cuOpt was not initially capturing, allowing for further system refinement.

#NVIDIA #Palantir #SupplyChain #cuOpt #Foundry

Source: From Wafer-Out to First Token: Codifying Supply Chain Expertise with Nemotron and Palantir Foundry | NVIDIA Technical Blog
